question: What does God inheriting what the man says mean?

positions.position: God takes the man's actual worldly wealth and children at death, ending his ownership of them.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid identifies al-ʿĀṣ's wealth and children (MUJAHID, YAḤYĀ, ṬABARĪ, IBN KATHĪR, DURR); Qatāda says all he possesses (YAḤYĀ, ʿABD AL-RAZZĀQ, ṬABARĪ, IBN KATHĪR, DURR). Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda and Ibn Zayd explain that destruction ends his ownership (WĀḤIDĪ, ṬABRISĪ, IBN AL-JAWZĪ); al-Zajjāj says it passes to others. Ibn Qutayba, Bayḍāwī, Bursawī and Ālūsī contrast real worldly goods with a baseless future boast; Ālūsī prefers this sense, reading mā as their substance. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls inheritance figurative dispossession, a threat of near death; his sons ʿAmr and Hishām became Muslims, bringing the Prophet good news and al-ʿĀṣ grief. Asad likewise calls it a metaphor for taking what had been vested in him. Al-Biqāʿī locates this at death; the Study Quran cites God as ultimate Inheritor (19:40, 15:23, 21:89, 28:58). Al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān mention the possibility that even hoped-for worldly goods, if granted, are later removed, comparing 6:94; Ālūsī finds that imagined grant very remote in light of the occasion report. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the failed hope an inherited disappointment.

positions.position: God deprives him of the wealth and children he claimed for the Hereafter and assigns them to others.
positions.reasons: Muqātil says the claimed reward goes to someone else; al-Farrāʾ chooses Paradise property for another. Al-Suddī and al-Kalbī specify gold, silver and silk for other Muslims (WĀḤIDĪ); Abū Suhayl says more deserving recipients (ABŪ ḤAYYĀN, ĀLŪSĪ). Ibn al-Jawzī reports Ibn ʿAbbās and says al-Farrāʾ selected it. Al-Kashshāf calls them the claimed goods given to someone deserving. Ālūsī says the interpretation presumes no procreation in Paradise. Wāḥidī adds that he also loses what he possessed here; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls the hope disappointed. Māwardī presents this beside the worldly-wealth account.

positions.position: God inherits everything the man amassed and did in worldly life.
positions.reasons: Ibn Zayd says nothing, small or great, accompanies him (ṬABARĪ and IBN KATHĪR); this extends the inherited object to his deeds as well as possessions.

positions.position: God preserves the man's utterance as a charge to be used against him at judgment.
positions.reasons: Al-Baghawī says it is retained for requital; al-Naḥḥās compares scholars inheriting prophets through preserving their words (IBN ʿAṬIYYA, ABŪ ḤAYYĀN). Al-Kashshāf says the record exposes and shames him at the gathering. Ālūsī observes that the earlier 'We shall write' already expresses preservation. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads the man's surviving claim as a sin attached to him, with no worldly support left; he prefers this because the passage seriously rebuts the claim.

positions.position: God ends the man's mocking speech when death overtakes him.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf says he speaks only while alive; Ālūsī says death reveals reality and ends further mockery. An objection that this assumes an unbeliever sincerely believed in resurrection is answered by saying mockery can continue until death.

positions.position: God inherits the man himself.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās gives this concise gloss, without further explanation in the note.

turns_on: Whether mā denotes real possessions, imagined Paradise goods, the man's entire legacy, his recorded words, his continuing speech, or the man himself; the occasion report and the prior promise to record his words are invoked in the discussion.

question: How is mā in 'We inherit him what he says' construed?

positions.position: Mā is an appositive of inclusion or clarification to the object pronoun.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn calls it an appositive of inclusion. Bursawī cites al-ʿUyūn for an appositional reading that accompanies his destruction and transfer of wealth and children. Ālūsī says it explains the pronoun; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it an appositional clarification of the object pronoun, whose referent is actual property and children.

positions.position: Mā is the direct object, with the attached pronoun implying 'from him'.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn and Ālūsī present this syntactic alternative.

positions.position: An omitted noun before mā means the sense or named referent of his words.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn reports this because words themselves cannot be inherited.

turns_on: The syntactic relation of mā to the object pronoun, and whether an omitted noun is needed because literal words cannot be inherited.

question: What does 'what he says' refer to?

positions.position: His boast that he would receive wealth and children in the Hereafter.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba, Ṭabarī, al-Farrāʾ, al-Nasafī, the Study Quran and others identify the claim of future wealth and children; Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the majority's reading as a sworn claim of Paradise goods after resurrection. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the short phrase compresses a lengthy boast and mockery and compares 3:183.

positions.position: His claim to receive wealth and children in worldly life.
positions.reasons: Bursawī says only the worldly goods actually given can be inherited, because the future boast has no object. Al-Kashshāf and Abū Ḥayyān entertain a hope for worldly wealth that could be granted and then removed; Ālūsī finds that suggestion remote given the occasion report. Ṭabāṭabāʾī's preferred account says he claimed disbelief would bring wealth and children and left that sinful claim behind.

positions.position: His full blasphemy and mockery, compressed into a short phrase.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the concise reference to hostile words in 3:183. Al-Kashshāf and Ālūsī take the speech literally as continued mockery until death.

turns_on: Whether the reported promise concerns goods in the next life or worldly goods, and whether the phrase includes the man's broader blasphemy and mockery.

question: Why does 'he says' use a present verb?

positions.position: Its sense recalls what the man already said.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān explicitly says the present form has past meaning. Ālūsī relates the tense to what the man had received; Ibn ʿĀshūr treats the expression as a compressed reference to his prior speech.

positions.position: It portrays his repeated speech while he lives, which death will stop.
positions.reasons: Al-Kashshāf and Ālūsī say the man keeps mocking while alive; death exposes reality and silences him.

turns_on: Whether the present form recalls an earlier claim or depicts ongoing mockery until death.

question: What variant wording is reported for 'We inherit what he says'?

positions.position: Ibn Masʿūd read it as God inheriting what the man has.
positions.reasons: ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr, al-Durr and Ālūsī transmit this reading; Wāḥidī and Ālūsī use it to clarify the interpretation of actual possessions, and al-Durr connects it to his solitary arrival.

question: What does coming to God alone mean?

positions.position: He arrives at resurrection without his wealth, children, or other worldly possessions.
positions.reasons: Muqātil, al-Farrāʾ, Ibn Qutayba, Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī and others describe an empty-handed arrival. Ibn Zayd says nothing small or great accompanies him. Al-Kashshāf says he loses both his coveted goods and his wish; on the first interpretation everyone initially arrives this way before later outcomes diverge. Al-Rāzī, al-Nasafī, al-Kashshāf and the Study Quran cite 6:94; the Study Quran also cites 19:95 and says the goods had supplied worldly honor and security. Bursawī says he has no goods from this life, still less an added share; Bayḍāwī also allows that he has abandoned his claim.

positions.position: He arrives without a defender, helper, clan, or any useful support.
positions.reasons: Māwardī offers this as an alternative to lacking wealth and children. Jishumī says a person deserving punishment has no helpful thing; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān stress humiliation and lack of supporters. Al-Qurṭubī mentions the clan; al-Biqāʿī adds lost honor and strength. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says only the preserved statement and its consequence accompany him. Asad says he must rely solely on God's grace and mercy, citing 6:94 and 19:95.

turns_on: Whether solitude stresses lost possessions and offspring or lost social and spiritual support; several sources include both.

question: What is the grammatical role of 'alone'?

positions.position: It is a circumstantial accusative describing his state on arrival.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās identifies the circumstantial construction. Ālūsī says it holds under all interpretations: future-oriented when wealth and children are transferred, otherwise simply his arrival alone.

question: Who is the man to whom the pronouns refer?

positions.position: Al-ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil.
positions.reasons: Mujāhid explicitly identifies him, as do the reports of Khabbāb's debt and al-Farrāʾ's explanation; Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this as one majority identification.

positions.position: Al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.
positions.reasons: Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports this as an alternative identification within the majority reading, without further evidence in the note.

turns_on: The reports identify al-ʿĀṣ; Ṭabāṭabāʾī also records al-Walīd as an alternative.

question: What happened to prompt the passage?

positions.position: Khabbāb sought payment from al-ʿĀṣ, who demanded that he renounce Muhammad and mocked repayment after resurrection from future wealth and children.
positions.reasons: Yaḥyā says Khabbāb told the Prophet before revelation; ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr and Bukhārī give the same core report. Al-Qurṭubī says Muslim and Bukhārī transmitted it; Ibn Kathīr notes several canonical routes. Al-Biqāʿī's Bukhārī version specifies Khabbāb forged a sword; al-Qurṭubī reports al-Kalbī and Muqātil's detail that the blacksmith made jewelry, with al-ʿĀṣ claiming Khabbāb had no greater Paradise entitlement. Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites similar reports from al-Ṭabarānī, Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr through al-Ḥasan and an unnamed Companion, and Ibn ʿAbbās, without grading them. Ṭabāṭabāʾī objects that a disbeliever's mockery of resurrection does not fit the passage's serious rebuttal.

positions.position: Companions sought debts from al-ʿĀṣ, who mocked their promised Paradise and said he too would have wealth, children, and a book there.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās gives this account in Ṭabarī; Ibn Kathīr transmits it by al-ʿAwfī. It differs from the Khabbāb account in the claim of a book and the companions' collective debt collection. Ṭabāṭabāʾī's contextual objection to mockery also bears on this account.

turns_on: Whether the event was Khabbāb's individual unpaid work or companions collecting debts, and whether mockery of resurrection fits a passage that answers the claim seriously.

question: Does Paradise include procreation?

positions.position: Its people have no offspring there.
positions.reasons: Ālūsī reports Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs and Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī denying procreation, citing reports that Paradise's people have no offspring and a long report from Laqīṭ ibn ʿĀmir. Ibn Mandah says only a denier or ignorant person rejects the Laqīṭ report. A report from Abū Dharr al-ʿUqaylī likewise says no child. Al-Safārīnī says most scholars favor no procreation and supplies ten arguments, though Ālūsī says many are debatable. The side answers opposing reports as excluding only ordinary worldly reproduction; al-Bayhaqī weakens the latter opposing report.

positions.position: A believer who wishes for a child in Paradise can have one, with rapid conception, birth and growth.
positions.reasons: Abū Saʿīd's Tirmidhī report says all stages occur in an hour; Tirmidhī calls it gharīb. Abū Nuʿaym transmits another report that a child is possible as soon as wished. Al-Safārīnī calls the Tirmidhī chain the best procreation report but notes inconsistent wording; Ālūsī says even a ḥasan conditional report need not mean the condition occurs and finds reconciliation weak. Al-Bayhaqī calls the latter report weak.

turns_on: The force and wording of the conditional Tirmidhī report, the reliability of the other report, and whether the no-child reports exclude all procreation or only ordinary reproduction.

question: What judgment does the verse make on the boast?

positions.position: The lie is recorded for added punishment, and the boaster loses every claimed advantage at judgment.
positions.reasons: Ṭabarī says he had neither knowledge of the unseen nor a covenant through faith and obedience: disbelief and the false boast bring increased punishment. Islāḥī says disbelief and arrogance draw escalating punishment, followed by empty-handed arrival. Bukhārī's report says the passage rejects the boast and foretells punishment and solitary return. Ibn al-ʿĀshūr calls the dispossession a threat of destruction; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the preserved sinful statement alone accompanies him to its consequence.

question: What inward lesson is drawn from his solitary return?

positions.position: Attachment to fortune, offspring, salvation and status breeds conceit and leaves a person unsupported; one must break that conceit.
positions.reasons: Bursawī describes deluded people who boast of worldly fortune and future rank while mocking renunciants; attachment distances them from God. He cites al-Kamāl al-Khujandī's couplet that breaking the idol of conceit in the lovers' faith is better than a hundred acts of worship.
